passages.source_text: θαρσήσαντες οὖν πρόσιτε τῷ θεῷ, οἱ τὴν ἀρχὴν ἐπὶ τῷ πάντων ἄρχειν καὶ κυριεύειν γεγενημένοι, οἵτινες ἔχετε αὐτοῦ ἐν μὲν τῷ σώματι τὴν εἰκόνα, ὁμοίως τε ἔχετε ἐν τῷ νῷ τῆς γνώμης τὴν ὁμοιότητα. ἐπεὶ οὖν ἀλόγοις ζῴοις ἐοικότα πράξαντες ἐκ τῆς ψυχῆς τὴν ἀνθρώπου ψυχὴν ἀπωλέσατε, ὥσπερ χοῖροι γενόμενοι δαιμόνων αἰτήματα ἐγένεσθε. ἐὰν οὖν τοῦ θεοῦ νόμον ἀναδέξησθε, ἄνθρωποι γίνεσθε. οὐ γὰρ οἷον ἀλόγοις ζῴοις ἐστιν εἰπεῖν „οὐ φονεύσεις, οὐ μοιχεύσεις, οὐ κλέψεις“ καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. διὸ μὴ φθονέσητε ἑαυτοῖς εἰς τὴν πρώτην ἀνακαλούμενοι εἰσελθεῖν εὐγένειαν. δυνατὸν γὰρ ἐστίν. ἐὰν τῷ θεῷ διὰ τῶν ἀγαθῶν πράξεων ἐξομοιωθῆτε: καὶ διὰ τὴν ὁμοιότητα υἱοὶ ἐκείνου εἶναι λογισθέντες πάντων δεσπόται ἀποκαταστῆναι δυνήσεσθε.

ἄρξασθε οὖν ἀποδύεσθαι τῶν κενῶν εἰδώλων τοὺς ἐπιβλαβεῖς φόβους, ὅπως τὴν ἄδικον φύγητε δουλείαν· δεσπόται γὰρ γεγόνασιν ὑμῶν ἐκεῖνοι, οἳ καὶ εἰς δούλους ὑμῖν ἄχρηστοι τυγχάνουσιν. λέγω δὲ περὶ ὕλης τῶν ἀψύχων ἀγαλμάτων τῶν μηδὲ πρὸς τὸ δουλεύειν ὑμῖν χρησιμευόντων. οὔτε γὰρ ἀκούει οὔτε βλέπει οὔτε αἰσθάνεται, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ μὴν κινηθῆναι δύναται. ἢ γὰρ βούλεταί τις ὑμῶν οὕτως ὁρᾶν ὡς ὁρᾷ καὶ ἀκούειν ὡς ἀκούει καὶ αἰσθάνεσθαι καὶ κινεῖσθαι; ἀλλ’ ἀπείη τοιαύτῃ λοιδορίᾳ λοιδορεῖν πάνθ’ ὁντινοῦν ἄνθρωπον, εἰκόνα περιφέροντα θεοῦ, εἰ καὶ τὴν ὁμοιότητα ἀπώλεσεν.

τοὺς γοῦν θεοὺς ὑμῶν τοὺς χρυσέους καὶ ἀργυρέους ἢ καὶ ἐξ ἄλλης τινὸς ὕλης γεγενημένους εἰς τὴν πρώτην αὐτῶν φύσιν ἀποκαταστήσατε, εἴς τε φιάλας λέγω καὶ λεκάνας καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ πάντα, ὅσα ὑμῖν πρὸς ὑπηρεσίαν χρήσιμα εἶναι δύναται· καὶ ταῦτα ὑμῖν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς δοθέντα ἀγαθὰ ἀποκατασταθῆναι δυνηθήσεται. ἀλλ’ ἴσως ἐρεῖτε Οὐκ ἐῶσιν ἡμᾶς τοῦτο ποιῆσαι οἱ τῶν ἐφεστώτων νόμοι. καλῶς ὅτι Νόμοι, καὶ οὐκ αὐτῶν τῶν εἰκαίων σεβασμάτων ἡ μὴ οὖσα δύναμις. πῶς οὖν αὐτοὺς θεοὺς νενομίκατε, ὑπὸ ἀνθρωπίνων νόμων ἐκδικουμένους, ὑπὸ κυνῶν φρουρουμένους, ὑπὸ μόχλων φυλασσομένους; καὶ ταῦτα ἐὰν χρύσεα ἢ ἀργύρεα ἢ χάλκεα· τὰ γὰρ λίθινα ἢ ὀστράκινα ὑπὸ τῆς ἀτιμίας φυλάσσεται, ὅτι οὐδεὶς ἀνθρώπων λίθινον ἢ ὀστράκινον ὀρέγεται κλέψαι θεόν. ὥστε μεγάλῳ κινδύνῳ ὑπόκεινται οἱ ἐκ πολυτελεστέρας ὕλης γεγενημένοι ὑμῶν θεοί. πῶς δὴ καὶ θεοί εἰσιν, κλεπτόμενοι, χωνευόμενοι, σταθμιζόμενοι, σφυρούμενοι;

ὦ τῶν ταλαιπώρων ἀνθρώπων φρένες, νεκρῶν νεκρότερα δεδιότων· οὐδὲ γὰρ νεκρὰ αὐτὰ λέγειν δύναμαι τὰ μηδέποτε ζήσαντα, εἰ μὴ ἐκτὸς τάφοι ἀρχαίων ἀνθρώπων εἰσίν. ἐνίοτε γὰρ ἐπιβάς τις ἀγνώστοις τόποις οὐκ οἶδεν οὓς ὁρᾷ ναούς, πότερόν ποτε νεκρῶν ἀνδρῶν μνήματά ἐστιν ἢ τῶν λεγομένων θεῶν· πυθόμενος δὲ καὶ ἀκούσας ὅτι θεῶν, προσεκύνησεν οὐκ αἰδεσθείς, ὅτι εἰ μὴ ἐξετάσας μεμαθήκει, διὰ τὸ ἴσον τῆς ὁμοιότητος ὡς νεκροῦ μνημεῖον ἂν παρεληλύθει. πλὴν οὐ χρή με πρὸς τὴν τῆς τοιαύτης δεισιδαιμονίας πολλὴν παρέχειν ἀπόδειξιν. ῥᾴδιον γάρ ἐστιν τῷ θέλοντι νοῆσαι ὅτι οὐδέν ἐστιν, ἐκτὸς εἰ μή τις οὐ βλέπει. πλὴν κἂν νῦν ἄκουσον ὅτι οὐκ ἀκούει, καὶ νόησον ὅτι οὐ νοεῖ. χεῖρες γὰρ αὐτὸ θανόντος ἀνθρώπου „ἐποίησαν“. εἰ δὲ ὁ ποιήσας ἐτελεύτησεν, πῶς τὸ ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ γεγονὸς οὐ λυθήσεται; τί οὖν θνητοῦ ἔργον προσκυνεῖς, παντελῶς ἀναίσθητον ὄν; ὁπότε οἱ λογισμοὺς ἔχοντες οὐδὲ τὰ ζῷα προσκυνοῦσιν οὐδὲ στοιχεῖα τὰ ὑπὸ θεοῦ γεγενημένα κολακεύουσιν, λέγω δὲ οὐρανόν, ἥλιον, σελήνην, ἄστρα, γῆν, θάλασσαν καὶ πάντα τὰ ἐν αὐτοῖς, ὀρθῶς κρίνοντες μὴ δεῖν τὰ ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ γενόμενα προσκυνεῖν, ἀλλὰ τὸν τούτων δημιουργὸν καὶ πάροχον σέβειν θεόν. ἐπὶ τούτῳ γὰρ καὶ αὐτὰ χαίρει ὅτι τὴν τοῦ πεποιηκότος τιμὴν οὐδεὶς αὐτοῖς προσῆψεν.

αὐτοῦ γὰρ μόνου ἐστὶν ἡ ἔντιμος δόξα τοῦ μόνου ἀγενήτου, ὅτι τὰ λοιπὰ πάντα γενητὰ τυγχάνει. ὡς οὖν τοῦ ἀγενήτου ἴδιον τὸ θεὸς εἶναι, οὕτως πᾶν ὁτιοῦν γενόμενον θεὸς τῷ ὄντι οὐκ ἔστιν. πρὸ πάντων οὖν ἐννοηθῆναι ὀφείλετε τὴν τοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν ἀπατῶντος ὄφεως κακοῦργον ἐπίνοιαν, ὃς φρονίμως ὑμᾶς ἀπατᾷ ὑποσχέσει κρείττονος λογισμοῦ, ἕρπων ὑμῶν ἐκ τοῦ ἐγκεφάλου εἰς τὸν νωτιαῖον μυελὸν καὶ μέγα κέρδος ἡγούμενος τὴν ὑμετέραν ἀπάτην.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: Take courage, then, and approach God—you who were made at the beginning to rule and exercise lordship over everything, who have his image in the body and likewise possess in the mind the likeness of will. Since, then, by doing things resembling irrational animals you lost from your soul the soul of a human being, you became like pigs and became what demons ask for. If, then, you accept God’s law, you become human beings. For it is not possible to say to irrational animals, “You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal,” and the rest. Therefore, do not begrudge yourselves entering your original nobility when you are called back to it. For it is possible. If you become like God through good deeds, then, having been reckoned his sons because of the likeness, you will be able to be restored as masters of everything.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν ἀρχὴν ἐπὶ τῷ πάντων ἄρχειν καὶ κυριεύειν γεγενημένοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: made at the beginning to rule and exercise lordship over everything
lexical_decisions.rationale: Treats τὴν ἀρχήν temporally and preserves the distinction between ἄρχειν and κυριεύειν.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν τῷ νῷ τῆς γνώμης τὴν ὁμοιότητα
lexical_decisions.chosen: possess in the mind the likeness of will
lexical_decisions.rationale: γνώμη can denote will, disposition, purpose, or judgment. “Will” fits the contrast between bodily image and mental or volitional likeness without adding an explicit possessive absent from the phrase.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δαιμόνων αἰτήματα ἐγένεσθε
lexical_decisions.chosen: became what demons ask for
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, “became requests of demons.” The contextual rendering treats αἰτήματα as the objects requested, likely invoking demons’ request concerning pigs; “became demons’ demands” is another possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μὴ φθονέσητε ἑαυτοῖς
lexical_decisions.chosen: do not begrudge yourselves
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the reflexive force and the sense of withholding a good from oneself.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάντων δεσπόται ἀποκαταστῆναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: be restored as masters of everything
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes πάντων with δεσπόται and retains the restoration motif established earlier in the section.

source_issues.source_quote: ἐκ τῆς ψυχῆς τὴν ἀνθρώπου ψυχὴν ἀπωλέσατε
source_issues.issue: The repetition of ψυχή produces the semantically unusual statement “you lost from your soul the soul of a human being.” The supplied reading is translatable and has been preserved rather than silently changed, though rhetorical paradox or textual disturbance remains possible.

passages.text: Begin, then, to strip off the harmful fears of empty idols, so that you may escape unjust slavery. For they have become your masters, though they are useless to you even as servants. I mean the material of the lifeless statues, which are of no use even in serving you. For it neither hears nor sees nor perceives; indeed, it cannot even move. Or does any of you wish to see as it sees, to hear as it hears, and to perceive and move? But far be it to insult any human being at all with such an insult, one who carries God’s image around, even if he has lost the likeness.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀποδύεσθαι τῶν κενῶν εἰδώλων τοὺς ἐπιβλαβεῖς φόβους
lexical_decisions.chosen: strip off the harmful fears of empty idols
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the clothing metaphor in ἀποδύεσθαι and allows the genitive to identify the idols that occasion or receive the fears.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἳ καὶ εἰς δούλους ὑμῖν ἄχρηστοι τυγχάνουσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: though they are useless to you even as servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idols are contrasted with the mastery wrongly granted to them: they would be useless even in the subordinate role of servants.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: λέγω δὲ περὶ ὕλης
lexical_decisions.chosen: I mean the material
lexical_decisions.rationale: The singular pronouns in the following sentence naturally refer to ὕλη, the statue’s inert material, rather than to the preceding plural statues.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὕτως ὁρᾶν ὡς ὁρᾷ καὶ ἀκούειν ὡς ἀκούει
lexical_decisions.chosen: to see as it sees, to hear as it hears
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the deliberately absurd comparison with the sight and hearing of insensible material.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀπείη τοιαύτῃ λοιδορίᾳ λοιδορεῖν πάνθ’ ὁντινοῦν ἄνθρωπον
lexical_decisions.chosen: far be it to insult any human being at all with such an insult
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the emphatic repudiation, the repetition of the λοιδορία word group, and the comprehensive force of πάνθ’ ὁντινοῦν.

passages.text: Restore, at any rate, your gods—those of gold and silver, or those made from any other material—to their original nature: to bowls, I mean, and basins and all the other things that can be useful in serving you. And these good things, given to you from the beginning, will be able to be restored to you. But perhaps you will say, “The laws of those in authority do not permit us to do this.” Good! It is laws, and not the nonexistent power of the vain objects of worship themselves. How, then, have you regarded as gods those who are defended by human laws, guarded by dogs, and secured by bars? And this is so if they are of gold, silver, or bronze; for the stone or earthenware ones are protected by their lack of value, because no human being desires to steal a stone or earthenware god. Thus your gods made from more costly material are exposed to great danger. How, then, are they even gods when they are stolen, melted down, weighed, and hammered?

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὴν πρώτην αὐτῶν φύσιν ἀποκαταστήσατε
lexical_decisions.chosen: restore ... to their original nature
lexical_decisions.rationale: The statues’ materials are to be returned to their prior, useful forms, preserving both φύσις and the restoration language.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἴς τε φιάλας λέγω καὶ λεκάνας
lexical_decisions.chosen: to bowls, I mean, and basins
lexical_decisions.rationale: φιάλη denotes a broad or shallow bowl, while λεκάνη denotes a basin; λέγω marks the author’s clarification.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ τῶν ἐφεστώτων νόμοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: the laws of those in authority
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐφεστῶτες are those standing over others, hence rulers or authorities; the less specific rendering preserves the source’s formulation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καλῶς ὅτι Νόμοι, καὶ οὐκ αὐτῶν τῶν εἰκαίων σεβασμάτων ἡ μὴ οὖσα δύναμις
lexical_decisions.chosen: Good! It is laws, and not the nonexistent power of the vain objects of worship themselves
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compressed retort contrasts the actual restraint of civil laws with the nonexistent power of the objects being revered. εἰκαῖος can mean vain, idle, or groundless.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ ἀνθρωπίνων νόμων ἐκδικουμένους
lexical_decisions.chosen: defended by human laws
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκδικέω in the passive can mean avenged, vindicated, or protected. “Defended” best fits laws preventing the statues’ destruction or removal.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ γὰρ λίθινα ἢ ὀστράκινα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the stone or earthenware ones
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὀστράκινος denotes material made from fired clay or earthenware, not merely an object shaped like a shell.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κλεπτόμενοι, χωνευόμενοι, σταθμιζόμενοι, σφυρούμενοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: stolen, melted down, weighed, and hammered
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves all four passive participles and the sequence of actions to which valuable metal images are subjected.

passages.text: Ah, the minds of wretched human beings, afraid of things deader than corpses! For I cannot even call things that have never lived dead—unless, that is, they are tombs of ancient people. Sometimes someone arriving in unfamiliar places does not know whether the temples he sees are memorials of dead men or of the so-called gods. But after asking and hearing that they belong to gods, he worships, without being ashamed that, if he had not learned by inquiry, he would have passed one by as a dead man’s monument because of the exact resemblance. Still, I need not contribute toward an extensive demonstration concerning superstition of this kind. For anyone willing to understand can easily grasp that it is nothing—unless someone does not see. Nevertheless, at least now hear that it does not hear, and understand that it does not understand. For the hands of a man who died “made” it. And if the one who made it came to his end, how will what came into being through him not be dissolved? Why, then, do you worship a mortal’s work, when it is entirely without sensation and people who possess reason do not even worship animals or pay court to the elements made by God—I mean heaven, sun, moon, stars, earth, sea, and everything in them—but correctly judge that they should not worship the things made by him, but should revere God, the creator and provider of these things? For these things themselves also rejoice in this: that no one has attached to them the honor belonging to the one who made them.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: νεκρῶν νεκρότερα
lexical_decisions.chosen: deader than corpses
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparative image is retained; νεκροί here naturally denotes dead persons or corpses rather than abstractly “the dead.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ μὴ ἐκτὸς τάφοι ἀρχαίων ἀνθρώπων εἰσίν
lexical_decisions.chosen: unless, that is, they are tombs of ancient people
lexical_decisions.rationale: Treats the stacked exceptive wording εἰ μὴ ἐκτός as emphatic. The alternative “unless perhaps” gives a similar contextual sense.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ τὸ ἴσον τῆς ὁμοιότητος
lexical_decisions.chosen: because of the exact resemblance
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally referring to the equality of the likeness, the phrase stresses that a temple and a tomb are indistinguishable in appearance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πλὴν οὐ χρή με πρὸς τὴν τῆς τοιαύτης δεισιδαιμονίας πολλὴν παρέχειν ἀπόδειξιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Still, I need not contribute toward an extensive demonstration concerning superstition of this kind
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes παρέχειν absolutely as “contribute” and πρὸς with the accusative phrase ending in ἀπόδειξιν as expressing the goal. The genitive τῆς τοιαύτης δεισιδαιμονίας identifies the demonstration’s subject matter. “Contribute toward an extensive exposition of superstition of this kind” is a viable alternative; the construction does not explicitly express proof “against” superstition.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πλὴν κἂν νῦν ἄκουσον
lexical_decisions.chosen: Nevertheless, at least now hear
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this exhortation κἄν has the concessive-minimal force “at least,” rather than introducing a full conditional clause.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: χεῖρες γὰρ αὐτὸ θανόντος ἀνθρώπου „ἐποίησαν“
lexical_decisions.chosen: the hands of a man who died “made” it
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the source’s quotation marking around the rendering of ἐποίησαν alone, while rendering the singular object αὐτό outside the quotation marks.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁπότε οἱ λογισμοὺς ἔχοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: when ... people who possess reason
lexical_decisions.rationale: The clause is attached to the preceding rhetorical question as a contrasting circumstance. It could instead be presented as a loosely independent “seeing that” or “whereas” sentence; the edition’s punctuation does not require emendation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐδὲ στοιχεῖα τὰ ὑπὸ θεοῦ γεγενημένα κολακεύουσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: do not ... pay court to the elements made by God
lexical_decisions.rationale: στοιχεῖα denotes cosmic elements or constituent parts of the world, while κολακεύω literally evokes flattering or courting them.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν τούτων δημιουργὸν καὶ πάροχον σέβειν θεόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: revere God, the creator and provider of these things
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάροχος can denote a provider, supplier, or giver. “Provider” preserves its distinction from δημιουργός, “creator.”

source_issues.source_quote: εἰ μὴ ἐκτὸς τάφοι ἀρχαίων ἀνθρώπων εἰσίν
source_issues.issue: The combination εἰ μὴ ἐκτός is unusually redundant as an exceptive expression. A defensible emphatic reading is available, so the supplied text is retained without conjectural correction.

source_issues.source_quote: πλὴν οὐ χρή με πρὸς τὴν τῆς τοιαύτης δεισιδαιμονίας πολλὴν παρέχειν ἀπόδειξιν
source_issues.issue: The printed order places πρός before an accusative phrase extending through ἀπόδειξιν, although παρέχειν can elsewhere take ἀπόδειξιν directly as its object. The translation provisionally takes παρέχειν absolutely, “contribute,” with the πρός phrase expressing the goal. The syntax is compressed and alternative construals such as “contribute toward an extensive exposition concerning this kind of superstition” remain possible, but no correction of the supplied text is required for a defensible translation.

passages.text: For glory worthy of honor belongs to him alone, the only unoriginated one, since everything else has come into being. Just as being God, then, belongs uniquely to the unoriginated one, so anything at all that has come into being is not truly God. Above all, therefore, you must understand the malicious scheme of the serpent that is deceiving you from within. It cleverly deceives you with the promise of better reasoning, crawling from your brain into your spinal marrow and regarding your being deceived as a great gain.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ ἔντιμος δόξα
lexical_decisions.chosen: glory worthy of honor
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔντιμος describes something honored, esteemed, or worthy of honor. The rendering avoids turning the adjective and noun into two separate source claims.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ μόνου ἀγενήτου
lexical_decisions.chosen: the only unoriginated one
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀγένητος is contrasted here with γενητός and γενόμενον, so “unoriginated” preserves the coming-into-being contrast more precisely than “unbegotten.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πᾶν ὁτιοῦν γενόμενον θεὸς τῷ ὄντι οὐκ ἔστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: anything at all that has come into being is not truly God
lexical_decisions.rationale: πᾶν ὁτιοῦν is emphatically comprehensive, while τῷ ὄντι means “in reality” or “truly.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν τοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν ἀπατῶντος ὄφεως κακοῦργον ἐπίνοιαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the malicious scheme of the serpent that is deceiving you from within
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐν ὑμῖν may describe either the serpent’s location or the sphere of its deception. “From within” preserves both possibilities without identifying the serpent with a specific anatomical structure.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: φρονίμως ὑμᾶς ἀπατᾷ ὑποσχέσει κρείττονος λογισμοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: cleverly deceives you with the promise of better reasoning
lexical_decisions.rationale: φρονίμως is ironic here and means intelligently or shrewdly; λογισμός may mean reasoning, calculation, or thought.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἕρπων ὑμῶν ἐκ τοῦ ἐγκεφάλου εἰς τὸν νωτιαῖον μυελὸν
lexical_decisions.chosen: crawling from your brain into your spinal marrow
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the anatomical image and the serpent’s downward movement from the brain into the spinal cord or marrow.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μέγα κέρδος ἡγούμενος τὴν ὑμετέραν ἀπάτην
lexical_decisions.chosen: regarding your being deceived as a great gain
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑμετέραν ἀπάτην could formally mean “your deception,” including deception practiced by you, but the repeated claim that the serpent deceives the audience favors the objective sense, their being deceived.

where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
